If it can't be phrased that way, you picked a policy — pick again. State where the truth of that claim physically lives today (config file, API, log, DB row, cloud setting).

Quality of falsifiability is judgment-dependent — structural presence is machine-checkable, semantic correctness needs rubric/LLM review.

lab_tasks.instruction: Score the control against all five legacy problems (§4.3): manual toil, transactional relationship, whack-a-mole, closed-framework focus, commoditized compliance — one honest sentence each. All five must be named by name; 'N/A' allowed only with a one-line justification.

' for each miss.

lab_tasks.instruction: Map the legacy arrow: in one or two sentences describe how this control is verified today, identify it as framework → controls → implementation → evidence → audit, and note where reality is consulted (usually last, by hand, periodically).

lab_tasks.machine_verify_check: Regex for the legacy arrow sequence (e.g. /framework.*(->|→).*audit/i or the words 'framework' and 'audit' in a Legacy-arrow section) plus a 'reality is consulted' phrase. lab_tasks.instruction: Map the engineered arrow: walk the SAME control through all seven loop stages — UNDERSTAND, LOCATE, QUERY, EVALUATE, EVIDENCE, MONITOR, OWN — one line each. LOCATE must name the actual system that holds the truth.
lab_tasks.objective: O1, O3
lab_tasks.machine_verify_check: Port of happy-path.sh logic: CASE-SENSITIVE match for each uppercase stage token ['UNDERSTAND','LOCATE','QUERY','EVALUATE','EVIDENCE','MONITOR','OWN']; hit count must equal 7 (S_HITS=7). lab_tasks.instruction: Close with a one-sentence inversion statement contrasting the two arrows for this specific control — what changes when reality drives the policy instead of the document.
lab_tasks.objective: O1
lab_tasks.machine_verify_check: Exact CI regex (case-insensitive, ERE): reality[[:space:]]*->[[:space:]]*policy|reality.*drive.*policy. On miss, emit '  missing reality->policy inversion statement'.

Keep it — Module 15 (capstone) re-opens this exact file.
lab_tasks.objective: O4
lab_tasks.machine_verify_check: File exists matching glob legacy-vs-engineered-*.md in the virtual filesystem; word count roughly 350-600; the full evaluate_analysis() port returns 0 (5/5 problems, 7/7 stages, inversion regex). Mirrors the CI's PASS line on success.

lab_setup_state: The learner-facing §6 lab assumes NO tooling — it is a writing exercise against a fixed template. The repo's executable assets are CI-side: labs/setup.sh [DEST_DIR] (default ./lab00) writes a conforming sample analysis to lab00/legacy-vs-engineered-laptop-encryption.md (the laptop-encryption worked example expressed in the required fixed shape); labs/happy-path.sh generates that fixture in a mktemp dir, additionally writes lab00/non-conforming.md (a 3-line legacy-only counterexample: 'We confirm laptops are encrypted by collecting screenshots each quarter for the auditor. That is all we do.'), and asserts the conforming sample passes and the non-conforming one is rejected. A browser sim should seed: ~/lab00/legacy-vs-engineered-laptop-encryption.md (calibration sample, read-only), ~/lab00/non-conforming.md (counterexample), and an empty editable ~/lab00/legacy-vs-engineered-<control>.md template with the five required section headings.
assessment_artifact: A one-page legacy-vs-engineered analysis (legacy-vs-engineered-<control>.md, ~350-600 words) of a control the learner actually owns: falsifiable claim + physical truth location; all five legacy problems scored by name; legacy-arrow description noting when/how reality is consulted; all seven loop stages mapped with a concrete named LOCATE; closing one-sentence inversion statement. Plus a short spoken or written defense that states the inversion thesis cold and connects at least one of the five principles to the legacy problem it answers. Graded Pass/Not-yet against rubric.md (6 rows, all must pass; Not-yet routes to a specific §4 section). The artifact is RETAINED — Module 15 capstone re-opens this exact file as the 'before' half of the program-long before/after.

exercise_design.sim_state: Virtual filesystem: ~/lab00/legacy-vs-engineered-laptop-encryption.md (read-only conforming exemplar, byte-identical to setup.sh output), ~/lab00/non-conforming.md (counterexample), and an editable ~/lab00/legacy-vs-engineered-<control>.md template pre-populated with the five required section headings. Plus authored data tables: the 5 problems, 5 principles, 8 'X over Y' values, legacy 5-stage arrow tokens, loop 7-stage tokens, and 4-6 scenario vignettes (including §5.3's quarterly-screenshot-email script).
exercise_design.notes: This is a mindset/writing module with zero learner-facing shell, so the highest-fidelity exercise is NOT a terminal — it is (a) concept drills and (b) writing the actual capstone-bound artifact against the exact CI validator. Proposed flow: [1] Arrow ordering — drag the legacy stages into framework→controls→implementation→evidence→audit and the loop stages into UNDERSTAND→…→OWN (deterministic check). [2] Principle↔problem matching — pair each of the 5 principles with the legacy problem it answers per §4.4 (deterministic; this is also the rubric's defense criterion). [3] Vignette classification — given short scenarios (e.g. §5.3's script that emails one screenshot quarterly), classify as legacy / commoditized-automation / engineered, and for engineered ones identify which loop stage each sentence implements (authored fixtures). [4] Claim-or-policy gate — given candidate sentences, accept only falsifiable 'X is true of system Y' claims (authored). [5-7] The artifact builder: a markdown editor for the one-page analysis with a 'Run rubric check' button that executes a JS port of evaluate_analysis() byte-for-byte — same case-insensitive substring checks for the 5 problem names (including the hyphenated 'closed-framework' and 'whack-a-mole'), same CASE-SENSITIVE uppercase stage tokens, same inversion ERE, emitting the CI's exact '  missing …' lines and the exact final PASS string. Optionally skin the validator as a one-command mock terminal ('bash happy-path.sh') for flavor — but a full shell-sim engine is unnecessary; all checks are trivial client-side string operations. Critically, let the learner ALSO run the check against non-conforming.md to see rejection, mirroring the CI's discrimination assertion. Export/download of the finished artifact is essential since Module 15 diffs against it.

fidelity_notes: Three judgment-dependent edges: (1) The CI rubric is purely structural/gameable — pasting the five problem names with no honest analysis passes grep; real grading of 'honest sentence per problem', 'falsifiable claim', and 'concrete LOCATE' needs human or LLM rubric review, so the sim should present its validator as the structural floor, not the grade. (2) Exact-output quirks to replicate: stage tokens are matched case-sensitive UPPERCASE (lowercase 'Locate:' fails), 'closed-framework' and 'whack-a-mole' must be hyphenated to match, and the inversion regex accepts either 'reality -> policy' (any spacing) or 'reality…drive…policy' case-insensitively; error lines are two-space-indented. (3) The spoken defense (state the thesis cold, link a principle to its problem) cannot be file-verified — exercise [2] approximates it as a matching drill. The legacy-arrow section (lab task 3) has NO corresponding CI check; any sim check there is an extension beyond ground truth. Conceptual mentions of MDM APIs / merge APIs / SQL are illustrative prose, not invocable commands — do not build them as terminal commands for this module.

assessment_artifact: From a FRESH, UNSEEN access export (assessor regenerates with different rows/roles/malformed line via `bash ../labs/setup.sh /tmp/assess01` + hand edits), unaided, within 30 minutes: (1) a re-runnable script taking the export path as a single argument that produces ONE evidence file answering a stated control question via composed small programs (no monolithic all-in-one tool), with collection errors separated into their own log via 2>, and that EXITS 0 EXACTLY WHEN THE CONTROL PASSES; (2) a spoken/written walkthrough identifying working directory and how they knew it, tracing one command through the REPL steps, explaining the pipe composition, the stdout/stderr separation, and the pass/fail meaning of the exit code. Scored against 7 binary rubric rows (Orientation, REPL fluency, Composition, Stream control, Verdict, Reproducibility, Explanation quality) — all must Pass; a Not-yet routes back to a specific concept section.

exercise_design.sim_state: xterm.js front-end over a POSIX shell engine with: virtual FS rooted at /, HOME=/home/analyst seeded with evidence/ reports/ scratch/; prompt template `analyst@workstation:{cwd-with-~-collapse}$ `; PATH containing coreutils (pwd ls cat grep wc echo awk chmod mkdir test man) + two authored fictional binaries: `lab-setup` (writes the exact 9-line access-export.csv fixture to ~/lab01 and echoes 'lab01 fixture written to ...') and `collect-encryption-status` (authored per-laptop stdout lines + stderr 'WARN: host db-07 unreachable'); ~/evidence/access.csv hypothetical export with zero legacy-admin rows for §5.3/5.4 verbatim replay; shell state tracking cwd, $?, command history, fd redirections (>, >>, 2>, |), executable mode bits, and the ability to execute learner-authored .sh files.
exercise_design.notes: Three-part flow. Part A (4 guided replay steps): learner reproduces worked examples 5.1-5.4 byte-identically in the sim — the verbatim outputs in the module are the gold transcript, so these double as fidelity tests. Part B (7 lab tasks): the §6 guided lab against the lab-setup fixture, each step machine-verified from VFS + history + exit codes as specified per task; verification checks OUTCOMES (file contents, pipeline shape, exit codes) not exact command strings, since the lab deliberately permits multiple correct pipelines. Part C (1 assessment exercise): the engine GENERATES a randomized fresh export (parameterized user/role rows, randomized malformed line, randomized expected count) and auto-grades the learner's script by (a) running it twice and diffing evidence, (b) running it against BOTH a passing and a failing mutation of the fixture and asserting exit 0 iff pass — this fully machine-verifies the hardest rubric rows (Composition, Stream control, Verdict, Reproducibility). KEY ENGINEERING DECISION: because task 7 and the assessment require executing arbitrary learner-written bash scripts, a hand-rolled pattern-matching shell sim is insufficient — use a real shell+coreutils compiled to WASM (busybox/bash + GNU coreutils) or a complete-enough interpreter; capture ground-truth transcripts by replaying every command in the fidelity manifest inside an ubuntu container against the seeded fixtures and snapshot-test the sim against them. Walkthrough/explanation rubric rows (REPL fluency, Orientation narrative, terminal-vs-shell origin story) are not deterministically machine-checkable — pair each with a short structured check (ordered-step sorting of the 6 REPL steps, multiple-choice on exit-code semantics) plus optional LLM grading of free text.

fidelity_notes: 1) GNU vs BSD divergence: module output is GNU-flavored — `wc -l` in a pipe prints bare '0' (BSD/macOS pads with leading spaces), so ground truth must come from docker-linux, not macos-host, despite the module permitting macOS Terminal. 2) `ls` output 'evidence  reports  scratch' assumes two-space column layout on one line, no color — sim must pin terminal width/colorless behavior. 3) Prompt fidelity is load-bearing: §4.1 and §5.1 teach reading the prompt (user@host:~$ with ~-collapse after cd), so the sim prompt must change exactly as shown. 4) Internal fixture inconsistency to handle: worked example §5.3/5.4 uses a hypothetical access.csv with ZERO legacy-admin rows (count 0, grep -q exit 1) while the lab fixture access-export.csv CONTAINS carol,legacy-admin — seed them as separate files or replay breaks. 5) `collect-encryption-status` stdout content ('one line per laptop') is unspecified — must be authored; only the stderr line is verbatim. 6) `lab-setup` is fictional (lab-container wrapper around labs/setup.sh) — authored fixture. 7) `man` output is paged and long; bundling real Ubuntu man pages is heavy — consider authored condensed pages, accepting a fidelity tradeoff, or ship real man page text without the pager. 8) `echo $?` requires the sim to maintain real per-command exit-code state including pipeline exit semantics (last stage). 9) Lab tasks accept many correct pipelines (grep pattern choice: 'admin' matches both admin and legacy-admin = 3; awk-based parsing is the reference for task 5) — verification must be outcome-based; the no-monolithic-tool rule needs a structural pipeline check (>= 2 pipes, distinct programs). 10) Free-text deliverables (4-6 sentence explanation, REPL walkthrough, terminal-vs-shell origin story) are judgment-dependent — exact-output fidelity does not apply; use structured proxies or LLM grading.

lab_setup_state: Two layers. (1) The real §6 lab assumes a fresh Linux instance the learner controls with sudo/root (lab VM, throwaway cloud instance, or local VM), a second SSH session kept open as lockout insurance, an SSH public key available to install, a default-ish /etc/ssh/sshd_config (containing commented decoys like '#PasswordAuthentication yes'), working systemd + journald, and a package manager with a small installable service. No grcops or intern users exist yet. (2) The repo's offline proxy: labs/setup.sh writes ./lab02-fixtures/ containing sshd_config (7 effective+decoy lines incl. '#PasswordAuthentication yes' decoy, 'PermitRootLogin no', 'PasswordAuthentication no'), id-grcops.txt ('uid=1001(grcops) gid=1001(grcops) groups=1001(grcops),27(sudo)'), and id-intern.txt ('uid=1002(intern) gid=1002(intern) groups=1002(intern)'); labs/happy-path.sh is the CI verifier asserting the control-evaluation logic (last-directive-wins parsing, sudo-group membership, composed COMPLIANT verdict) with bash+coreutils only. A browser sim should seed: hostname web-01, users root/grcops(1001)/intern(1002), group sudo gid 27, /home/grcops/.ssh/{authorized_keys (seeded 644 — over-permissioned on purpose), id_ed25519 (411 bytes, 600)}, /etc/ssh/sshd_config (3243 bytes, root:root 640, with decoy lines), a systemd unit registry (ssh active+enabled; evidence-collector installable), an apt package DB, and a journal that gains 'May 27 09:31:54 web-01 sshd[1402]: Accepted publickey for grcops from 10.0.0.5' after a simulated key login.
assessment_artifact: evidence-writeup.md — a one-page compliance-evidence writeup produced unaided in 60 minutes on a fresh, unseen Linux instance. For each of the three hardening controls (named non-root sudo admin + non-privileged account two-sided; SSH effective PasswordAuthentication no / PermitRootLogin no resolved as sshd parses; a service both active (running) and enabled), the block must contain: control statement, exact copy-pasteable command, the specific evidence line(s) of output, and a one-sentence pass/fail verdict — plus backing raw outputs (both id outputs, decoded ls -l of .ssh material, resolved effective directives, two-field systemctl status, and the journalctl 'Accepted publickey' line with no successful password login). Pass requires every control both implemented and defensibly evidenced such that an assessor re-running each command reaches the identical verdict; graded against the 7-row rubric (all rows must pass, each routing to a §4/§5 section on Not-yet).

exercise_design.sim_state: Single simulated Ubuntu host 'web-01' with a stateful virtual filesystem (the /etc, /var/log, /home, /usr convention must be real and navigable), a user/group database (/etc/passwd, /etc/group with sudo gid 27), per-file mode/owner/size/mtime metadata driving byte-identical ls -l, a process table (sshd PID 742 running as root), a systemd unit registry with active/enabled flags driving systemctl status/start/stop/enable/disable/reload output, a journald store that appends auth events when simulated SSH logins occur, an apt package DB supporting list --installed and installing one small service, and /etc/ssh/sshd_config pre-seeded with the commented decoy '#PasswordAuthentication yes' above real directives. State mutations: useradd/usermod rewrite passwd/group; chmod rewrites mode bits; config edits (via sed/tee/echo-append or a simplified built-in editor) rewrite the file; systemctl flips unit flags; a 'connect from second terminal' button triggers the scripted ssh handshake that appends the journal line.
exercise_design.notes: The most realistic exercise is a two-pane experience: a stateful Linux terminal sim (left) where the learner actually hardens web-01 through the 8 lab tasks, and an evidence-writeup builder (right) — a structured form with per-control fields (statement / command / evidence line / verdict) that the engine machine-diffs against live sim state, exactly mirroring the assessment artifact. Signature set pieces: (a) the §5.3 decoy trap — seed the commented '#PasswordAuthentication yes' and grade the naive grep as a teachable failure, only accepting a comments-stripped last-wins resolution (the repo's happy-path.sh awk logic IS the reference verifier, portable to JS verbatim); (b) the active-vs-enabled trap — seed the installed service as started-but-not-enabled after task 6's start step so the learner must notice 'disabled' in status and run enable, then answer the reboot-consequence question; (c) the two-sided id check — intern must be checked too, not just grcops; (d) the over-permissioned authorized_keys (644) forcing a real chmod with ls -l re-render. Permission-string decoding (§4.5/§5.2) is a perfect standalone matching/mapping micro-exercise: show a ten-character string + a user, learner gives the r/w/x verdict — generate dozens of variants programmatically. Fidelity strategy: capture golden outputs once from a systemd-enabled Ubuntu 24.04 container (or VM) seeded with the exact scenario values (users 1001/1002, gid 27, file sizes 3243/411, frozen May 27 2026 timestamps, PID 742/1402), then replay from the sim's state model. Interactive ssh/sudo flows are scripted dialogues, not real auth. The 60-minute assessment can reuse the identical engine with a freshly randomized host (different usernames, decoy placement, service name, seeded perms) so it is genuinely unseen.

fidelity_notes: Hard fidelity items: (1) systemctl status and journalctl output formatting varies by distro/version (bullet glyph, cgroup/Memory/CPU lines, journal date formats) — standard docker containers have no systemd, so golden capture needs a systemd-enabled container (privileged, /sbin/init entrypoint) or a real VM; pin one distro (Ubuntu LTS) and note Ubuntu's unit is 'ssh' while RHEL's is 'sshd', and auth.log vs /var/log/secure. (2) The evidence-collector unit is fictional — author its unit file in the capture environment so the status output is real, but the module's shown output (timestamps 'Wed 2026-05-27 09:14:02 UTC') is authored scenario data the sim must pin. (3) All module outputs embed scenario constants the sim must seed exactly for byte-identical match: hostname web-01, IP 10.0.0.5, PIDs 742/1402, uid 1001/1002, gid 27(sudo), file sizes 3243/411 bytes, May 27 timestamps. (4) ps column widths are content-dependent — reproduce padding rules. (5) Interactive flows (ssh key vs password login, sudo password prompt, editing sshd_config in nano/vim) cannot run for real in a static web app — script the handshakes; for editing, support sed/tee/append or a deliberately simplified editor, since a faithful vim is out of scope. (6) apt install transcript is long and version-pinned — author one frozen transcript from the capture container. (7) systemctl status exit codes (0 active, 3 inactive) matter if the verifier checks exit codes. Judgment-dependent grading: lab task 8's writeup quality and task 6's reboot-consequence sentence need keyword or LLM-rubric grading rather than exact match; everything else is deterministically checkable, and labs/happy-path.sh's awk parsers (effective_directive, in_sudo_group) are the canonical verification logic to port to the browser engine.

fidelity_notes: High overall fidelity is achievable: all validator outputs in this manifest were captured by actually running validate-coverage.ts under bun against the committed fixtures (2026-06-12). (the §4.5 lognormal caveat as a reflection question); (4) RAG-grid demolition mini-exercise — given a 5x5 colored grid and two priced options ($200k high vs 2×$50k mediums), show the grid cannot answer which to fund, then answer it with the sampler; (5) product-card structured builder with machine checks (one owner, prioritized customers, ranked backlog, metrics incl. $ exposure); (6) seven-stage scoring table builder reusing happy-path.sh's exact assertions (7 stages, valid calls, hard-fail UNDERSTAND/OWN != BUILD); (7) boundary builder forcing BOTH a vendor-wins and an owning-wins entry (the anti-NIH/anti-vendor-worship check is structural); (8) policy-exception scenario — vendor dashboard shows 'FAIL: unencrypted disk' for a risk-accepted public-data server; learner picks the defensible response (encode exception in owned policy layer vs manual quarterly override); (9) memo assembly — concatenate the artifacts into decision-memo.md and verify the recommendation cites the computed dollar figure. Free-text paragraphs (boundary, recommendation, tail rationale) need keyword/rubric heuristics or an optional LLM-grader; everything else is fully deterministic.

fidelity_notes: Two fidelity classes here. (1) expected_loss.ts is fully deterministic (LCG seed 42) and platform-independent — exact fixture output is mean=493516, tailValue=1133873; module §5.2 rounds these to ~$494,000 and ~$1,134,000. Port the LCG verbatim to the sim for perfect fidelity, and recompute exactly when the learner edits ranges. (2) happy-path.sh's awk path is NOT portable-deterministic: awk's srand(42)/rand() differs across implementations (macOS awk produced mean=$491867, p95=$1126125; gawk on Linux will produce different numbers). The script is designed for this — it asserts a ±5% band around the analytic mean (0.35 × 1,400,000 = $490,000) and tail>mean, never exact values. A sim reproducing happy-path.sh should either pin one implementation's verbatim PASS line (e.g., the macOS one above, or run once under gawk in docker for a Linux-canonical line) or render the PASS line from the sim's own sampler values, since any mean in [465500, 514500] with tail>mean is a legitimate run. Also note one inconsistency to avoid teaching as gospel: setup.sh defaults DEST to ./fixtures relative to CWD, so running it from the repo root vs labs/ writes to different paths — the sim should mirror the lab convention (run from labs/, fixture at labs/fixtures/risk-input.json). The committed fixture and the setup.sh-generated fixture are byte-identical. All free-text deliverables (boundary paragraph, recommendation) have no machine-exact ground truth — grade structurally (both-directions present, dollar figure cited, EVALUATE named) plus keyword heuristics.

lab_setup_state: setup.sh writes a starter capstone repo at ./capstone-lab (pure bash+coreutils+awk; no network, cloud, Docker, or yq): capstone-manifest.yaml (complete fixture: S3 public-access control, owner a.engineer@example.com, all 7 stages mapped, before_after: before-after.md); placeholder artifacts each manifest entry resolves to — control-statement.md (claim + threat + four public-access-block ground-truth fields), collect.sh (executable, echoes '{"buckets":[]}'), policy/public_access.rego (package capstone.public_access; default allow := false), evidence/.keep, .github/workflows/ccm.yml (name: ccm, cron '0 */6 * * *'), README.md (customers/owner/backlog x3 with known gap/metric/UX), before-after.md (4-dimension table + legacy problems #1/#5 + residual gap); and validate-capstone.sh (executable awk/grep coverage validator, exit 0/1/2 semantics). A second fixture, capstone-manifest-incomplete.yaml (MONITOR key and before_after pointer absent), is used for the negative case. setup.sh echoes the absolute lab dir path.
assessment_artifact: Terminal assessment of the entire curriculum — a shipped control repository for one real control plus before-after.md, independently reproduced by a DIFFERENT reviewer from a clean checkout: (1) capstone-manifest.yaml mapping all 7 loop stages to real artifacts + a validator the reviewer runs that exits 0; (2) an end-to-end pipeline where the scheduled/monitored path invokes the same QUERY→EVALUATE→EVIDENCE code as the manual run and produces the verdict the evidence claims; (3) README.md treating the control as a product (customers, single accountable owner, backlog with >=1 honest known gap, success metric, UX rationale); (4) before-after.md comparing the same control on >=4 concrete dimensions, scored against the 5 legacy-GRC problems, with >=1 residual gap cross-referenced to the backlog; (5) a walkthrough mapping all 7 stages, arguing trustworthiness from the before/after and live monitoring, and honestly diagnosing thin coverage. Rubric (7 rows, all must Pass, Pass/Not-yet with section routing): Loop coverage (O1,O5 -> §4.1-4.2,§5.1), End-to-end integration (O2 -> §4.3), Control-as-product (O3 -> §4.4), Before/after rigor (O4 -> §4.5,§5.3), Critical diagnosis (O5 -> §4.3,§5.4 — distinguishing done from claimed, e.g. logging mistaken for monitoring), Trust argument (O6 -> §3,§2), Reviewer reproduction (O2,O5 -> §4.6). Key reviewer rule: a stage claimed in the manifest but not actually satisfied (e.g. a MONITOR that collects but never evaluates or alerts) is Not-yet on Coverage regardless of what the manifest says.

exercise_design.sim_state: A simulated capstone repo filesystem seeded exactly from setup.sh output (9 files incl. the complete manifest fixture), plus the incomplete manifest fixture for the negative/diagnosis exercises. State tracked: file contents (manifest YAML, control-statement.md, README.md, before-after.md, ccm.yml, collect.sh, rego policy), executable bits, validator invocation history with exit codes, validator file hash (to detect gate-gaming), and an evidence/ directory that accumulates run-<timestamp>.json records when the learner runs the pipeline. The terminal-sim implements validate-capstone.sh faithfully: awk-style loop_coverage block parsing, per-stage ok/MISSING lines with exact column alignment ('  %-11s ok  -> %s'), the two MISSING variants ('no artifact mapped' vs 'artifact not found: <path>'), before/after check, and exit codes 0/1/2.
exercise_design.notes: This is a synthesis module, so the most realistic exercise is a 'ship the spine' simulation in four phases mirroring the lab. Phase A (matching-mapping warm-up): drag each of 9 candidate artifacts onto the 7 loop stages for the S3 public-access control (§5.1 coverage table) — includes distractors like 'a screenshot in a drive' and 'a parallel copy of collect.sh in the workflow' to test stage understanding. Phase B (terminal-sim + code-editor): start from the INCOMPLETE manifest in the seeded repo; learner runs ./validate-capstone.sh, reads the named gaps (MONITOR MISSING, before/after MISSING), then fixes them by editing capstone-manifest.yaml and creating .github/workflows/ccm.yml and before-after.md in the editor — re-running until PASS + exit 0, then running twice for reproducibility. Crucially, the sim must allow (and detect) the anti-pattern of editing the validator: if the learner modifies validate-capstone.sh, give targeted feedback that gaming the gate is the exact failure the program teaches against. Phase C (structured-builder): fill the control-as-product README (customers / single owner — reject team aliases / 3 backlog items with >=1 known-gap flag / metric / UX sentence) and the before/after table (4 dimension rows, 5 legacy-problem scores, 1 residual gap that must cross-reference a Phase C backlog item — enforce the cross-ref mechanically). Phase D (critical diagnosis, the §5.4 skill): present a peer's submission — manifest claims all 7 stages, but the ccm.yml schedule only runs collect.sh and uploads output, never invoking the rego policy or alerting; learner must mark MONITOR as 'claimed but not satisfied' and select the correct fix ('wire the existing EVALUATE into the scheduled path') from options that include plausible wrong fixes ('add more logging', 'increase schedule frequency', 'write a second policy for the scheduled path' — the last being the seam anti-pattern). The validator's exact transcript is the gold thread through the whole exercise: every phase ends with the learner predicting or producing the validator verdict line.

fidelity_notes: All lab tooling is pure bash+coreutils+awk by design (no yq, no cloud, no network, no Docker), so terminal-sim fidelity is highly achievable — the validator was executed on the macOS host and its full transcripts captured verbatim for both fixtures (validator output is identical on Linux; only mktemp paths differ). Three fidelity caveats: (1) module.md §5.2 shows the before/after check as one line ('checking before/after... ok -> before-after.md') but the real validator prints it as two lines ('checking before/after...' then '  before/after ok -> before-after.md') — the sim should match the real validator, and exercise answer-checking should not regex against the module's abbreviated transcript; (2) the per-stage output uses printf '  %-11s ok  -> %s' — two leading spaces, stage name left-padded to 11 chars, TWO spaces after 'ok' — happy-path.sh greps '^  ${stage} +ok  ->' so alignment is load-bearing; (3) evidence/run-<timestamp>.json, the rego evaluation (opa eval), and the GitHub Actions scheduled run are described but never executed by the lab fixtures — the placeholder collect.sh emits '{"buckets":[]}' and the rego is a stub (default allow := false); any sim that has the learner actually run the QUERY→EVALUATE→EVIDENCE pipeline (lab task 4) must author plausible opa/jq outputs as fixtures since the module shows no verbatim output for that path. The real capstone targets the learner's own environment (AWS S3, real OPA, real GitHub Actions) which a static web app cannot reproduce — the exercise should explicitly frame itself as the coverage-spine scaffold, exactly as the lab does.
